anchorPassages.note: Urgent prayer for rescue that the Exodos will answer with ruin instead.
anchorPassages.text:
Oh, as thou lov’st this city best of all,
To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken,
In our dire need we call;
Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken.
Thy ready help we crave,
Whether adown Parnassian heights descending,
Or o’er the roaring straits thy swift way wending,
Save us, O save!
Brightest of all the orbs that breathe forth light,
Authentic son of Zeus, immortal king,
Leader of all the voices of the night,
Come, and thy train of Thyiads with thee bring,
Thy maddened rout
Who dance before thee all night long, and shout,
Thy handmaids we,
Evoë, Evoë!

weDoAnswers: Dionysus was the god of theatre: tragedies were performed at his festival in Athens. The hymn is part of the play. Read closely: “Where Ismenus rolls his waters, Where the Dragon’s teeth were sown, Where the Bacchanals thy daughters Round thee roam, There thy home; Thebes, O Bacchus, is thine own.” (Chorus, lines 1062–1067).
analysis.weDoWords: “Ismenus”, “Dragon’s teeth” and “thine own” stand out in lines 1062–1067. The places named are Thebes’s own river and founding myth, so the elders claim Dionysus as the city’s god and ask him to come home and help. “Thebes, O Bacchus, is thine own” makes the appeal a claim of belonging.

Today's words: revellers — people taking part in a noisy celebration; bastion — a strong defensive position; clustered — gathered in close groups; sicken — to become ill; orbs — spheres, especially of light; rout — a disorderly crowd.

Dionysus was the god of theatre: tragedies were performed at his festival in Athens. The hymn is part of the play. Hope rises just before the catastrophe, a tragic pattern that also appears in Oedipus Rex. Structure: A brief choral prayer stands between Creon’s change of mind and the Messenger’s report, the calm before the ruin. Watch for burial and the unburied body: The hymn never names the corpse; its hope for healing sits beside the still-unburied Polyneices and the still-entombed Antigone.

segments.script: Today we saw how allusion shapes hymn to Dionysus. Key takeaway: The city that enforced Creon’s edict now begs a god to heal it, so divine help is asked only after human law has already done its harm.

lecture.note: Taught as a 20-minute preview at the start of the next section's lesson, not as a separate 90-minute class.

objective: Students will summarize what happens in Stasimon 5 (lines 1054–1093) (hymn to Dionysus) in 2 sentences and, in a 3-sentence warm-up response, explain how one quoted line from the scene sets up the scene that follows.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.text: Why ask Dionysus in particular to heal Thebes?
items.lookFor: Dionysus is Thebes’s own god; cite the local place-names in the hymn.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The elders ask Dionysus because Thebes is “thine own”: they name Ismenus and the place “Where the Dragon’s teeth were sown,” and they call the Bacchanals “thy daughters” (lines 1062–1067). He is the city’s own god, child of a Theban line, so they ask him in particular to come home and heal the land.

items.text: What does “Stasimon 5 (lines 1054–1093)” suggest about hymn to Dionysus? State the inference and the line that supports it.

items.answerGuidance: Hope rises just before the catastrophe, a tragic pattern that also appears in Oedipus Rex. Evidence to accept: “Thou by many names adored, / Child of Zeus the God of thunder, / Of a Theban bride the wonder, / Fair Italia’s guardian lord; / In the deep-embosomed glades / Of the Eleusinian Queen” (Stasimon 5, lines 1054–1061): Chorus, lines 1054–1061. Credit any reading that quotes the text and explains it.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.
